questions.prompt: State the principal argument interval used for a non-zero complex number \(z\).
questions.answer:
The principal argument is written \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)\).
It is chosen in the interval
\[
-\pi < \operatorname{Arg}(z) \le \pi.
\]
The number \(z=0\) has no argument because it has no direction from the origin.

questions.prompt: Give one argument of the complex number \(3i\).
questions.answer:
The point \(3i\) is at \((0,3)\), directly above the origin on the positive imaginary axis.
The angle from the positive real axis is
\[
\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
So one argument is \(\pi/2\).

questions.prompt: Find \(\operatorname{Arg}(-4)\).
questions.answer:
The complex number \(-4\) is the point \((-4,0)\) on the negative real axis.
The angle from the positive real axis to this ray is \(\pi\).
Since \(\pi\) is included in \((-\pi,\pi]\),
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(-4)=\pi.
\]

questions.prompt: Find \(\operatorname{Arg}(2-2i)\).
questions.answer:
The point \((2,-2)\) lies in quadrant IV.
The reference angle satisfies
\[
\tan \alpha=\left|\frac{-2}{2}\right|=1,\quad \alpha=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
In quadrant IV the principal argument is negative, so
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(2-2i)=-\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]

questions.prompt: Find the principal argument of \(-3+3i\).
questions.answer:
The point \((-3,3)\) lies in quadrant II.
The reference angle is
\[
\tan^{-1}\left|\frac{3}{-3}\right|=\tan^{-1}(1)=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
Quadrant II angles have form \(\pi-\alpha\), so
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(-3+3i)=\pi-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]

questions.prompt: Find the principal argument of \(-5-5\sqrt{3}i\).
questions.answer:
The point is in quadrant III.
The reference angle satisfies
\[
\tan \alpha=\left|\frac{-5\sqrt3}{-5}\right|=\sqrt3,\quad \alpha=\frac{\pi}{3}.
\]
A quadrant III direction may be written \(\pi+\pi/3=4\pi/3\), but this is outside \((-\pi,\pi]\).
Subtract \(2\pi\):
\[
\frac{4\pi}{3}-2\pi=-\frac{2\pi}{3}.
\]
Therefore \(\operatorname{Arg}(-5-5\sqrt3 i)=-2\pi/3\).

questions.prompt: Write the general argument of \(1+i\) using an integer parameter.
questions.answer:
The point \((1,1)\) lies in quadrant I and has reference angle
\[
\tan^{-1}(1)=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
The principal argument is \(\pi/4\).
All arguments differ by full turns of \(2\pi\), so
\[
\arg(1+i)=\frac{\pi}{4}+2k\pi,\quad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]

questions.prompt: Find the principal argument of \(\sqrt3-i\), giving the answer in radians.
questions.answer:
The point \((\sqrt3,-1)\) lies in quadrant IV.
The reference angle is
\[
\alpha=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6}.
\]
Because the imaginary part is negative and the real part is positive, the principal argument is
\[
-\alpha=-\frac{\pi}{6}.
\]

questions.prompt: A complex number has modulus \(6\) and principal argument \(-2\pi/3\). Find its Cartesian form.
questions.answer:
Use \(z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\).
Here \(r=6\) and \(\theta=-2\pi/3\).
\[
\cos\left(-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)=-\frac12,\quad \sin\left(-\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)=-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
z=6\left(-\frac12-i\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)=-3-3\sqrt3 i.
\]

questions.prompt: Find all \(\theta\in[0,2\pi)\) such that \(\theta\) is an argument of \(-2i\).
questions.answer:
The number \(-2i\) lies on the negative imaginary axis, so a direction angle is \(-\pi/2\).
To express this in \([0,2\pi)\), add \(2\pi\):
\[
-\frac{\pi}{2}+2\pi=\frac{3\pi}{2}.
\]
There is only one representative in the interval, so
\[
\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}.
\]

questions.prompt: Explain why \(\arg(z)\) is multi-valued but \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)\) is single-valued for \(z\ne0\).
questions.answer:
A ray from the origin has the same direction after any whole number of full turns.
If \(\theta\) is an argument of \(z\), then
\[
\theta+2k\pi
\]
is also an argument for every integer \(k\).
Thus \(\arg(z)\) represents infinitely many angles.
The principal argument \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)\) chooses exactly one of those angles by requiring
\[
-\pi<\operatorname{Arg}(z)\le\pi.
\]

questions.prompt: A student says \(\operatorname{Arg}(-1-i)=5\pi/4\). Diagnose the error and give the correct principal argument.
questions.answer:
The angle \(5\pi/4\) points to quadrant III, so it is an argument of \(-1-i\).
However, a principal argument must lie in
\[
(-\pi,\pi].
\]
Since \(5\pi/4>\pi\), subtract \(2\pi\):
\[
\frac{5\pi}{4}-2\pi=-\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(-1-i)=-\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]

questions.prompt: Find \(\operatorname{Arg}\left((1+i)(-\sqrt3+i)\right)\) without first fully expanding the product.
questions.answer:
Arguments add under multiplication, with the result adjusted to the principal interval.
For \(1+i\),
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(1+i)=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
For \(-\sqrt3+i\), the point is in quadrant II with reference angle \(\pi/6\), so
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(-\sqrt3+i)=\pi-\frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{5\pi}{6}.
\]
Add:
\[
\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{3\pi}{12}+\frac{10\pi}{12}=\frac{13\pi}{12}.
\]
This is greater than \(\pi\), so subtract \(2\pi\):
\[
\frac{13\pi}{12}-2\pi=-\frac{11\pi}{12}.
\]

questions.prompt: Let \(z\) have \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)=3\pi/4\). Find the principal argument of \(-iz\).
questions.answer:
Multiplication by \(-i\) rotates a complex number by \(-\pi/2\).
So an argument of \(-iz\) is
\[
\frac{3\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{3\pi}{4}-\frac{2\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]
This already lies in \((-\pi,\pi]\), so
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(-iz)=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]

questions.prompt: For which real values of \(t\) is \(\operatorname{Arg}(t+i)=\pi/4\)?
questions.answer:
The number \(t+i\) is the point \((t,1)\).
For principal argument \(\pi/4\), the point must lie on the ray making angle \(\pi/4\), where
\[
\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\frac{\text{imaginary part}}{\text{real part}}=\frac{1}{t}.
\]
Since \(\tan(\pi/4)=1\),
\[
1=\frac{1}{t},\quad t=1.
\]
This is in quadrant I, so it satisfies the required argument.

questions.prompt: For which real values of \(a\) does \(a-2i\) have principal argument \(-\pi/2\)?
questions.answer:
The argument \(-\pi/2\) is the negative imaginary axis.
A point on that axis has real part \(0\) and negative imaginary part.
For \(a-2i\), the real part is \(a\) and the imaginary part is \(-2\).
Thus we need
\[
a=0.
\]
The imaginary part is already negative, so \(a=0\) is valid.

questions.prompt: Find all real \(x\) such that \(\operatorname{Arg}(x+xi)=3\pi/4\).
questions.answer:
The point is \((x,x)\).
If \(x>0\), it lies in quadrant I and has argument \(\pi/4\).
If \(x<0\), it lies in quadrant III and the principal argument is
\[
-\frac{3\pi}{4},
\]
not \(3\pi/4\).
If \(x=0\), the number is \(0\), whose argument is undefined.
Therefore there are no real values of \(x\) satisfying the condition.

questions.prompt: Prove that for any non-zero complex number \(z\), \(\operatorname{Arg}(-z)\) is obtained from \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)+\pi\) by adjusting into \((-\pi,\pi]\).
questions.answer:
Multiplication by \(-1\) rotates every non-zero complex number by \(\pi\) radians.
If \(\theta=\operatorname{Arg}(z)\), then an argument of \(-z\) is
\[
\theta+\pi.
\]
Arguments that differ by \(2k\pi\) describe the same ray, so all arguments of \(-z\) are
\[
\theta+\pi+2k\pi,\quad k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
The principal argument is the unique one of these values lying in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
Thus \(\operatorname{Arg}(-z)\) is exactly \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)+\pi\) adjusted by a multiple of \(2\pi\) into the principal interval.

questions.prompt: A non-zero complex number \(z\) satisfies \(\operatorname{Arg}(z)=\theta\). Determine \(\operatorname{Arg}(1/z)\) in terms of \(\theta\), including the endpoint case.
questions.answer:
Write \(z=r e^{i\theta}\) with \(r>0\) and \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\).
Then
\[
\frac1z=\frac1r e^{-i\theta}.
\]
So an argument of \(1/z\) is \(-\theta\).
If \(-\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\), then \(\operatorname{Arg}(1/z)=-\theta\).
The only endpoint problem occurs when \(\theta=\pi\). Then \(-\theta=-\pi\), which is not allowed in the principal interval. Add \(2\pi\):
\[
-\pi+2\pi=\pi.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(1/z)=\begin{cases}-\theta,& -\pi<\theta<\pi,\\ \pi,& \theta=\pi.\end{cases}
\]

questions.prompt: Show why \(\operatorname{Arg}(z_1z_2)\) is not always equal to \(\operatorname{Arg}(z_1)+\operatorname{Arg}(z_2)\), even though arguments add under multiplication.
questions.answer:
Arguments add before the result is reduced to the principal interval.
Take
\[
z_1=z_2=-1+i\sqrt3.
\]
Each has principal argument \(2\pi/3\).
The sum of principal arguments is
\[
\frac{2\pi}{3}+\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{4\pi}{3}.
\]
But \(4\pi/3\) is not in \((-\pi,\pi]\). The principal representative is
\[
\frac{4\pi}{3}-2\pi=-\frac{2\pi}{3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Arg}(z_1z_2)=-\frac{2\pi}{3}\ne\frac{4\pi}{3}.
\]
The correct rule is to add arguments and then adjust by a multiple of \(2\pi\) into the principal interval.
